walkthrough.title: IBM Bob Quantum Experience Walkthrough
walkthrough.subtitle: Discover how IBM Bob empowers anyone to create quantum circuits with zero prior coding experience.
walkthrough.overview_desc: In this walkthrough, you'll see how IBM Bob acts as your patient AI pair-programmer. From turning plain ideas into quantum circuits to catching mistakes and running on simulators, Bob does the heavy lifting so you can focus on learning.
walkthrough.cap1_challenge: Quantum computing tutorials are often full of intimidating mathematical jargon and complex syntax. Beginners don't know where to start.
walkthrough.cap1_prompt: Hey Bob, I've never programmed before. Can you write a simple Qiskit circuit that flips a quantum coin with 50/50 odds, and explain what each line does?
walkthrough.cap1_explanation: Bob creates a clean 3-line circuit using QuantumCircuit, applies the Hadamard (h) gate to spin the coin into superposition, adds a measurement, and explains each line using the spinning coin analogy.
walkthrough.cap1_value_trad: Traditional: Hours spent reading linear algebra textbooks and wrestling with syntax.
walkthrough.cap1_value_bob: With Bob: 30 seconds to working, well-explained code.
walkthrough.cap2_challenge: Old tutorials from 2021 use deprecated functions like qiskit.execute() that break on modern Qiskit 2.x. Beginners get stuck on confusing error messages.
walkthrough.cap2_prompt: I found this old code online: 'execute(qc, Aer.get_backend("qasm_simulator"))'. Why doesn't it work, and how do I update it to modern Qiskit?
walkthrough.cap2_explanation: Bob identifies the obsolete function, explains that modern Qiskit uses Primitives (SamplerV2 / StatevectorSampler), and rewrites the code to current 2026 production standards.
walkthrough.cap2_value_trad: Traditional: Frustration over incompatible packages and deprecated APIs.
walkthrough.cap2_value_bob: With Bob: Instant automatic modernization to official Qiskit 2.x patterns.
walkthrough.cap3_challenge: Beginners wonder: 'What order do I run things? How does quantum code connect to normal computer charts?'
walkthrough.cap3_prompt: Bob, what is the complete step-by-step flow to create, run, and view the results of an entangled Bell state?
walkthrough.cap3_explanation: Bob organizes the workflow into 4 simple beats: 1. Build circuit -> 2. Entangle with CNOT -> 3. Run on local simulator -> 4. Plot counts bar chart.
walkthrough.cap3_value_trad: Traditional: Fragmented scripts without clear pipeline structure.
walkthrough.cap3_value_bob: With Bob: Clear 4-step pipeline that anyone can follow.
walkthrough.cap4_challenge: Beginners often forget essential steps, like measuring qubits or assigning classical registers, resulting in empty or confusing outputs.
walkthrough.cap4_prompt: Bob, check my circuit before I run it: qc = QuantumCircuit(2); qc.h(0); qc.cx(0,1). Is anything missing?
walkthrough.cap4_explanation: Bob catches the missing measurement gates: 'Your qubits are entangled, but you haven't added measurement gates! Without measuring, the classical computer cannot read the outcome. Add qc.measure_all()!'
walkthrough.cap4_value_trad: Traditional: Silent failures or cryptic runtime errors.
walkthrough.cap4_value_bob: With Bob: Shift-left detection catches errors before execution.
walkthrough.cap5_challenge: Understanding where quantum code runs: do you need an expensive quantum computer just to get started?
walkthrough.cap5_prompt: Explain the difference between running on my laptop simulator versus a real IBM Quantum computer.
walkthrough.cap5_explanation: Bob uses the Flight Simulator analogy: your laptop CPU computes the math for free with zero queue time. When you are ready for real hardware, you use the exact same code with IBM Quantum Runtime.
walkthrough.cap5_value_trad: Traditional: Fear of breaking expensive hardware or wasting compute credits.
walkthrough.cap5_value_bob: With Bob: Safe, confident prototyping locally with 1-click cloud escalation.
walkthrough.cap6_desc: Real-time metrics demonstrating your progress and developer confidence:

whyBob.modal_heading: Why IBM Bob Over Other Agentic Tools?
whyBob.modal_intro: Bob's strongest differentiation combines IBM legacy platform depth, enterprise-grade deployment control, and structured hybrid workflows. Here's where it wins most clearly:
whyBob.card_legacy_body: Bob for Z and Bob for i ship purpose-built agentic workflows for COBOL/PL/I refactoring, RPG modernization, business rule extraction, and Db2 for i SQL strategy — zero prompt engineering required.
whyBob.card_air_gapped_body: Deploy fully self-hosted on Red Hat OpenShift. Supports air-gapped image mirroring, LDAP/Keycloak identity, ISO 27001 compliance, and IT fleet governance via MDM/GPO group policies.
whyBob.card_devsecops_body: Scan against OWASP ASVS, output SARIF files for GitHub Advanced Security and CI/CD, and generate OSCAL POA&M remediation maps — structured for downstream AI agent consumption.
whyBob.card_acp_body: Bob Shell speaks Agent Client Protocol — the LSP of coding agents. Any ACP editor gets Bob's full runtime: model access, MCP servers, and shell execution. Swap editors freely.
whyBob.card_hybrid_body: Workflows interleave open-ended agentic steps with deterministic non-agentic operations, reducing token cost and producing consistent, predictable results for enterprise use cases.
whyBob.card_modes_body: Ask / Plan / Agent modes enforce capability scoping per task. Ask reads only; Plan writes plans, not code; Agent can run commands. Auditable and controllable in regulated environments.

intro.title: Quantum Experience Lab
intro.body: Hands-on quantum computing with IBM Bob + Qiskit

arc.title: Today's arc
arc.body: Two threads, one loop: quantum concepts, and IBM Bob as your pair-programmer for building them. We'll end by answering the real question — when is quantum actually faster, and can an AI help you build the circuit that proves it?

meet_bob.title: Meet IBM Bob
meet_bob.body: IBM Bob is an agentic assistant — it doesn't just answer, it calls tools. MCP (Model Context Protocol) lets Bob reach a Qiskit Code Assistant to write and explain real circuits — the same tool, whether it's running on your own machine or on a shared remote server — with you in the loop the whole way.

qubit.title: What is a Qubit?
qubit.body: A qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a classical bit, it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1 simultaneously.

superposition.title: Superposition
superposition.body: Applying a Hadamard gate puts a qubit into equal superposition — equal probability of measuring 0 or 1.

measurement.title: Measurement & statistics
measurement.body: Measuring a qubit collapses it to a classical 0 or 1 — but a single shot only tells you the outcome, not the odds. Repeat the same circuit many times and the histogram of outcomes converges to the true probabilities.

entanglement.title: Entanglement
entanglement.body: Two entangled qubits share a quantum state — measuring one instantly determines the other, regardless of distance.

gates.title: Gates & circuits
gates.body: A circuit reads left to right: gates (X, H) act on wires (qubits), a two-wire gate like CNOT entangles them, and a meter measures. Learning to read this diagram is what lets you — and Bob — talk about a circuit precisely.

ask_bob.title: Ask Bob to build it
ask_bob.body: Live: ask Bob to build the Bell circuit. Bob calls the MCP tool explain_circuit — the same Qiskit Code Assistant wired into Bob's MCP config — and returns working Qiskit code plus a plain-language explanation.

run_read.title: Run & read it
run_read.body: The code Bob wrote runs locally on the Aer simulator. The result: a counts histogram peaked at 00 and 11 — Bob reads it back as "these two qubits are correlated, never 01 or 10."

classical_parity.title: Classical parity check
classical_parity.body: Say a hidden function returns a single parity bit from several inputs. Classically there's no shortcut: you query it once per input, tallying results as you go, before you can compute the parity.

quantum_parity.title: Quantum parity check
quantum_parity.body: Put the same inputs in superposition and query the oracle once. Phase kickback writes the answer into every branch's phase at once; interference collects it into a single, certain outcome. Same answer, one query instead of many — this oracle trick is exactly what Grover generalizes next.

sim_vs_qpu.title: Simulator vs real QPU
sim_vs_qpu.body: Everything so far ran on Aer, a classical simulator — fast, free, noiseless. IBM Quantum backends are real superconducting qubits: same Qiskit code, but subject to real decoherence and gate error. The same run_via_backend() call picks the target; with an IBMQ_API_TOKEN set, the same circuit can target real hardware.

oracle_search.title: The oracle & search
oracle_search.body: Grover generalizes the parity trick to search: an oracle phase-flips the amplitude of the state(s) that satisfy your problem, then diffusion reflects every amplitude about the mean, amplifying the marked one. Repeat ~π/4·√N times and the answer dominates — a quadratic speedup over checking N possibilities one by one.

sat_oracle.title: Build a SAT oracle with Bob
sat_oracle.body: Capstone: pick a small boolean formula. Ask Bob — reaching the Qiskit Code Assistant MCP, whether it's running on your laptop or a shared remote server — to author the PhaseOracle that marks its satisfying assignment. Run Grover on the simulator and watch the histogram converge on the answer, verified against a classical brute-force check.

uc1_coin.title: Use case 1: a quantum coin from plain English
uc1_coin.question: Which gate puts one qubit into an equal mix of 0 and 1?
uc1_coin.explain: The Hadamard gate makes the fair coin.
uc1_coin.takehome: Prompt: Make a quantum coin and run it 1000 times. File: coin.py. Rule: modern Qiskit, with a measurement.

uc1_coin_two_qubits.title: What if: two coins that always match
uc1_coin_two_qubits.question: What counts will two entangled coins give?
uc1_coin_two_qubits.takehome: Prompt: /qiskit-beginner-circuit two coins that always land the same way. File: twins.py (Hadamard on one qubit, then a CX gate). Result in this run: only 00 and 11 appeared.

uc2_explain_docs.title: Use case 2: Bob explains a circuit with the Qiskit docs
uc2_explain_docs.question: In bell.py, what does the CX (CNOT) gate do to the second qubit?
uc2_explain_docs.choice0: Flips it only when the first qubit is 1
uc2_explain_docs.explain: CX flips the target qubit when the control qubit is 1. After H on the first qubit, that links the two.
uc2_explain_docs.takehome: Prompt: Explain bell.py gate by gate and link the docs page for each gate. Needs: the qiskit-docs MCP server (uvx qiskit-docs-mcp-server), no account.

uc2_no_docs.title: What if: the same question without the docs tool
uc2_no_docs.question: With no docs tool, where will Bob's links and facts come from?
uc2_no_docs.choice2: A local model on this laptop
uc2_no_docs.explain: No fetch happened. The links come from memory; they use the old docs.quantum.ibm.com address, which redirects. Nothing was checked.
uc2_no_docs.takehome: Same prompt, docs MCP off. The explanation is fluent but uncited and unchecked, so verify the links.

uc3_migrate_skill.title: Use case 3: migrate old Qiskit code with a skill
uc3_migrate_skill.question: Moving deutsch_jozsa.py from Qiskit 1.x to 2.x, what changes?
uc3_migrate_skill.choice0: The oracle and gate code are rewritten
uc3_migrate_skill.choice1: Only the Sampler call and how results are read
uc3_migrate_skill.explain: Only the primitive changes: the V1 Sampler is gone in 2.x. The circuit stays as it is. Note the skill is built for qiskit-ibm-runtime; Bob said so, then applied the equivalent change.
uc3_migrate_skill.takehome: Prompt: /migrate-qiskit-ibm-runtime Migrate deutsch_jozsa.py to the latest Qiskit release. Skill from github.com/Qiskit/skills. Cost on this run: about 1.2 Bobcoins, because the skill reads a large rules registry.

uc3_migrate_docs.title: What if: the same migration with the docs tool, no skill
uc3_migrate_docs.question: Where does Bob find the replacement API here?
uc3_migrate_docs.choice0: The Qiskit docs, through the MCP server
uc3_migrate_docs.explain: It searched the docs, fetched the V1 to V2 guide, and edited the file. Same result, about a fifth of the cost.
uc3_migrate_docs.takehome: Prompt: Migrate deutsch_jozsa.py to the latest Qiskit release (2.x). Use the Qiskit documentation to find the replacement APIs. Needs: the qiskit-docs MCP server.

uc4_sim_to_qpu.title: Use case 4: from simulated code to a real quantum computer
uc4_sim_to_qpu.question: Run on a real QPU, what will the constant oracle return?
uc4_sim_to_qpu.explain: Mostly 000 (1002 of 1024 shots) with a few wrong results. Real hardware has noise; the simulator does not.
uc4_sim_to_qpu.takehome: Prompt: adapt dj_sim.py to run on a real IBM quantum computer with qiskit-ibm-runtime. Needs: an IBM Quantum account (the free Open Plan works, 10 minutes of QPU time), the token in QISKIT_IBM_TOKEN, never in the code. This replay ran two small jobs on ibm_kingston.

athome.title: Do this at home
athome.intro: Everything in the recorded sessions, so you can repeat it at your own pace on your own account. The sessions ran on IBM Bob 2.0.9 and Qiskit 2.6.2 in November 2026.
athome.download_note: Contains the Bob config (.bob/mcp.json), three skills, a beginner-mentoring rule, the example scripts, the five lab notebooks and a README-HOME.md with the same steps as this page.
athome.need_account: An IBM Bob account. IBM lists a 30-day trial with 50 Bobcoins that needs an IBMid; check the current terms at ibm.com/products/ai-coding-agent/pricing.
athome.need_runtime: Node.js 24 or later, and Python with uv.
athome.need_qpu: For the last example only: a free IBM Quantum account (Open Plan, 10 minutes of QPU time per 28 days) and its API token.
athome.expect_body: Bob words things differently each time; the results should match: about 500 and 500 for the coin, a docs-linked explanation, the script running on Qiskit 2.x, and a real quantum computer giving mostly the right answer with a little noise.
